newsitem.title: FINLAND: CONFIDENCE SEEN RETURNING TO NOKIA IN '97.
newsitem.headline: CONFIDENCE SEEN RETURNING TO NOKIA IN '97.

text.p: The year 1997 is set to start on a much more positive note for Europe's largest mobile phone maker Nokia Oy than this year, analysts say.

About this time last year Nokia ran into sudden logistics woes which dragged its mobile phones unit into the red. Its stock plunged as the fast-track firm used to beating even the most bullish hopes shocked investors with a profit warning.
But now two subsequent quarterly reports have lived up to management's promises, and analysts see investor confidence growing next year as mobile phone margins recover.
"Nokia is now out of the penalty box. They've picked up the ball and are running very fast indeed," said Jeremy Alun-Jones, analyst at Lehman Brothers in London.
In the early 1990s, Nokia enjoyed a dominant position in mobile phones -- but besides its own "growing pains" late last year, 1996 was the year when new challengers started to emerge.
For next year, analysts are for now cautiously convinced by Nokia's assurances that it is again beefing up margins -- and will be looking ahead to assess its potential in multimedia.
PROFIT MARGINS RECOVER
Nokia, which did not quantify the extent of mobile phones losses in the first quarter, said it returned to profit in Q2 and by Q3 margins were consistent with the year-ago period.
CEO Jorma Ollila said in November Nokia expected double-digit margins in Mobile Phones, and was close to that level. In 1995, the division's operating profit was 10.9 percent of net sales.

The mobile phones unit's year-on-year net sales growth continued strong at 58 percent in January-September this year and Nokia has launched new products including a multi-purpose wireless telephone, the Nokia 9000 Communicator.

"Disbelief will keep ebbing as Nokia shows normal performance as it has in the two previous quarters, but I guess the events of late 1995 will not be forgotten," said Gunnar Andersson, analyst at Handelsbanken in Stockholm.
Last week Nokia briefed European analysts, who said the presentation reinforced hopeful views, although none reached by Reuters planned to change their near-term outlook.

Merita Bank analyst Martti Larjo said he would increase forecast growth rates for mobile handset markets around the turn the century since it seemed that once penetration is above 15 percent, it accelerates and does not stop at 30 percent.
"It could even rise as high as 100 percent in current high penetration areas," he said.
He predicted some subscribers would have several handsets -- for instance one in the car, one as a portable voice phone and a third for mobile data transfer.
STILL SCOPE FOR REVALUATION

Handelsbanken's Andersson said Nokia's share price -- which has risen 50 percent so far this year to around 260 markka against a 40 percent gain for the Helsinki index as a whole -- could trade at 327 markka a year from now based on fundamentals.

NatWest analyst Ian Macleod forecast Nokia's EPS at 10.4 markka this year and at 16.5 markka next, saying he expected to see margins above the normal level until the second half of the year when new rivals would join the handset competition seriously.
"(But) I would not expect another collapse in margins ... I think they've done a very good job of resolving their internal problems in handsets," he said.
In the three first quarters of this year, Nokia's EPS was 5.70 markka compared to 10.50 markka in the year-ago period.
According to consensus forecasts from Edinburgh Financial Publishing, Nokia's EPS is expected to rise to 14.90 markka next year from a forecast 10.0 markka this year.
As viewed on Reuters Securities 3000, the forecasts show a sharp reversal in trends two months ago with upgrades kicking in again after downgrades held sway earlier this year.

Various forecasts collected by Reuters put Nokia now at between 15 and 17 times 1997 earnings -- compared with Macleod's prospective average of 21 for the sector, comprising also Motorola , Ericsson , Northern Telecom and Lucent Technologies .
"There is potential for improved confidence in the management and it could be seen in a higher rating next year," said Macleod, who rates Nokia a "buy" at current levels.

Nokia's 4.93 billion markka 1995 pretax profit consisted mainly of a 2.72 billion operating profit in telecommunications and 1.75 billion in mobile phones, with 537 million in other units -- including its fledgling multimedia business.
CONTINUED STRENGTH IN INFRASTRUCTURE
Analysts expect Nokia to continue to post strong profits in mobile infrastructure solutions and say while growth could slow in Europe, Nokia is establishing itself on other markets.
"There has been a shift towards the Asia-Pacific region. (Nokia is) doing surpisingly well there," said Lehman's Alun-Jones, who also rates the stock "outperform".
Nokia posted 26 percent net sales growth in the third-quarter -- below expectations, which made some analysts fear it was losing market share to Ericsson .
But Nokia told analysts at the briefing it is not losing market share in infrastructure and margins remained strong, said Alun-Jones; adding he would believe this for a quarter.
And NatWest's Macleod said Nokia has a strong orderbook in infrastructure which supports positive expectations for next year, although this year's growth rate would be "closer to 30 than 40 percent".
"Next year will be more of the same," he said.
MULTIMEDIA POTENTIAL SEEN SHOWING 1998

Analysts agree Nokia has great potential as a supplier of multimedia platforms, in which it is a pioneer, but add that since the potentially enormous global market has not yet emerged, its scope is not yet discounted in the stock.
But they do not expect this to be an issue until the year after next.

"The market will not get going until 1998," said Merita's Larjo, but added that Nokia has considerable potential with its set-top multimedia platform to combine television network, personal computer and Internet services.
The market will not price even this into Nokia's stock until it can clearly be seen how the market develops and whether Nokia can make profits, he added.
"Nokia is at the top," he said. "But competition will become very fierce."
The technology is a lot simpler than mobile phones, he said: television makers and computer hardware manufacturers would be able to relatively quickly make rival products.
Also in 1997, analyst expect Nokia's rivals to catch up in new products linking mobile phones with computers -- like Nokia's Communicator and data cards.
